title: GETTING HELP IN RED HAT ENTERPRISE LINUX
display: Ch 4 — GETTING HELP IN RED HAT ENTERPRISE LINUX

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 4, pages 101–123. Guided Exercises: Reading Manual Pages, Reading Info Documentation. Lab: Getting Help in Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Why this chapter matters for the exam, specifically

The RHCSA exam gives you access to man pages during the test — there's no requirement to memorize every option of every command. What IS graded is your speed at finding the right flag under time pressure. Treat this chapter as exam-day survival skill, not just background reading.

man topic opens the manual page for topic, one screen at a time. Man pages are organized into numbered sections by content type — the same name can exist in more than one section, so the section number disambiguates:
| Section | Content |
| 1 | User commands |
| 2 | System calls (kernel routines) |
| 3 | Library functions |
| 4 | Special files (device files) |
| 5 | File formats (config file layouts) |
| 6 | Games |
| 7 | Conventions, standards, protocols, misc. |
| 8 | System administration / privileged commands |
Linux kernel API

The classic example: passwd(1) is the command to change a password; passwd(5) documents the /etc/passwd file's format. man passwd (no section) shows section 1 by default — man 5 passwd forces section 5.
Navigating once you're inside a man page
| Key | Action |
| Space / PageDown | Scroll forward one screen |
| PageUp | Scroll back one screen |
| `↑` / `↓` | Scroll one line |
| `/string` | Search forward for string |
| `n` / `Shift+N` | Repeat the search forward / backward |
| `g` / `Shift+G` | Jump to start / end of the page |
| `q` | Quit back to the shell |
NOTE — Search strings are regular expressions

A search string is actually a regular expression, not plain text — characters like $ * . ^ have special meaning. Searching for something containing those characters can give surprising results; that's a topic for RH134, but worth knowing why an odd search sometimes misbehaves.
Every man page follows roughly the same layout — you'll get faster by knowing which heading to jump to instead of reading top to bottom:
| Heading | What's there |
| `NAME` | One-line description |
| `SYNOPSIS` | The command's syntax summary |
| `DESCRIPTION` | Full explanation |
| `OPTIONS` | Every flag, explained |
| `EXAMPLES` | Worked examples |
| `FILES` | Related files/paths |
| `SEE ALSO` | Related man pages |
Finding the right man page when you don't know the command name
man -k keyword # search titles/descriptions for keyword
man -K keyword # full-text search (slower, more thorough)

man -k relies on an index built by mandb (runs automatically once a day, or shortly after boot if overdue) — if a page you just installed doesn't show up in a search yet, that index just hasn't caught up.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — man -k in practice

This is the fastest way to find a command you know exists but can't remember the exact name of — e.g. man -k "file system" when you need the tool that resizes an ext4 filesystem (turns out to be resize2fs) but can't recall it under pressure.

Some packages — especially GNU tools like coreutils — ship a second, more comprehensive documentation format called Info, viewed with pinfo. Where a man page is a short, formal reference for one command, Info documents are a whole hyperlinked book for a package, with a full-text search and a browsable index across topics.
| pinfo key | man equivalent | Action |
| PageDown / Space | PageDown / Space | Scroll forward one screen |
| `d` | (none) | Jump to the directory of topics |
| `u` | (none) | Go up to the parent node |
| `↓` then Enter | (none) | Follow a hyperlink |
| `/string` then Enter | `/string` | Search |
| `q` | `q` | Quit |

pinfo topic jumps straight to a topic; plain pinfo opens the top-level directory. If no Info node exists for what you asked for, pinfo falls back to showing the man page instead — so it never leaves you empty-handed.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. man passwd, then man 5 passwd — compare the command page to the file-format page.
2. man -k "ext4" — find the tool used to resize an ext4 filesystem (resize2fs) and the one to tune its parameters (tune2fs).
3. man -k zip — see how many unrelated tools share "zip" in their description; note why a specific, well-chosen keyword saves time over a vague one.
4. pinfo coreutils, then navigate into a subtopic like "Disk usage" to compare Info's style to a man page's.
5. whereis passwd — see every location (binary, man pages) associated with a single command name.
1. Q1 — You need the file-format documentation for /etc/crontab, not the crontab command itself. What do you type?
2. Q2 — man -k reports nothing for a command you just installed minutes ago, even though man <command> works fine directly. Why?
NOTE — Answers
Q1 — man 5 crontab (file formats live in section 5; man crontab alone would show the command's section-1 page by default).

Q2 — man -k searches the mandb index, which only rebuilds once a day (or shortly after boot) rather than instantly on install — the direct man <command> lookup doesn't depend on that index at all, which is why it still works.
- man topic (optionally man <section> topic) reads a manual page; section numbers disambiguate identical names across content types (1=commands, 5=file formats, 8=admin commands, etc.).
- man -k keyword searches the mandb-built index by title/description when you don't know the exact command name.
- pinfo gives package-level, hyperlinked documentation for GNU tools, and falls back to the man page if no Info node exists.
- You're allowed to use these during the RHCSA exam — practicing fast navigation now is time you get back on exam day.
